questions.prompt: What is special about the outer shell of a noble gas atom?
questions.explanation: Noble gases have completely full outer shells — 2 electrons for helium and 8 for the others — which is the most stable arrangement an atom can have.
questions.misconception: It's the alkali metals that have a single lonely electron in their outer shell — the noble gases are the ones with the full set, which is why they are so calm.

questions.prompt: How reactive are the noble gases?
options: The most reactive family of all
questions.explanation: Because their outer shells are already full, noble gases have no reason to gain, lose, or share electrons — so they almost never react.
questions.misconception: It's natural to think every gas is reactive, but the noble gases are the opposite extreme — their full shells mean there is simply nothing to react with.

questions.prompt: Which group of the periodic table are the noble gases?
questions.explanation: The noble gases fill Group 18 — the final column of the periodic table, at the far right.
questions.misconception: Group 1 is the alkali metals and Group 17 is the halogens — the noble gases specifically occupy that last, far-right column.

questions.prompt: Why is argon used to fill some lightbulbs?
options: Because it is unreactive and won't damage the bulb
Because it makes the bulb brighter
Because it is the cheapest liquid
Because it burns to create light
questions.explanation: Argon's calm, unreactive nature means it won't react with the hot filament inside the bulb, so the bulb lasts longer.
questions.misconception: The noble gases don't burn or glow by themselves (neon glows only when electricity passes through it) — their value inside a bulb is simply that they do nothing and react with nothing.
